meta.description: Professional experience at GenAIus Technology: roles, work areas and measured outcomes.
meta.note: Written at skill-and-outcome level. Internal architecture, route names, specific vulnerability details and client specifics are deliberately excluded.

entries.title: Professional experience
entries.text: I'm a Software Development Engineer at GenAIus Technology, a startup building an AI operating system. I joined as a Python Developer Intern in January 2026 and converted to full-time in July 2026 through a pre-placement offer. I work remotely. My work spans backend infrastructure and security hardening, AI/ML integration including RAG and multimodal model serving, and the node-based workflow platform users build on.

entries.title: What GenAIus Technology does
entries.text: GenAIus is a startup building an AI operating system — a platform where technical and non-technical users compose AI workflows as graphs of nodes. You connect a retrieval node, a model generation node, a custom logic node, and the platform runs them with data flowing between. The pitch is building domain-specific tools without writing code, with models runnable on hardware you control rather than API-only.

entries.title: SDE at GenAIus (Jul 2026 – present)
entries.text: Full-time since July 2026, converted from my internship. My remit is backend infrastructure on a large production Python system: security hardening, performance work, model integration and platform features. Recently: overhauled the file transfer pipeline, ran a hardware benchmarking framework across 15+ models and three platforms, set up vision, ASR, TTS and video-generation models on server GPUs, and led the migration from bespoke nodes to a reusable generic node system.
aliases: what does he do at work

entries.title: Security hardening on a production backend
entries.text: A major piece of my work. I audited a large Python backend systematically — tracing request paths end to end rather than spot-checking — then refactored file-path resolution and error handling to close filesystem-level vulnerabilities, and added validation at the gateway boundary so malformed input is rejected before it reaches business logic. Every fix shipped with regression tests: 80+ assertions on the path-handling changes alone. I also fixed a systemic issue where the gateway returned HTTP 200 for every error, which had been silently breaking monitoring, retries and CDN caching.

entries.title: File transfer pipeline overhaul
entries.text: The upload and download path had two failure modes: browser hangs on hundreds of files, memory spikes on large ones. I rebuilt it — backend uploads now stream to a temp file in fixed chunks with a size cap and single-pass integrity digest instead of buffering in memory, and the frontend got a bounded-concurrency queue with cancellation and batched cache writes. Results: a 300MB upload went from about 1,225MB of gateway memory to 2.6MB, a 470x reduction, and a 200-file operation went from 200 storage writes to one.

entries.title: Hardware benchmarking framework
entries.text: I designed and ran a benchmark comparing 15+ vision and text models across a laptop CPU, cloud T4 GPUs and server-class workstation GPUs, with platform detection, per-model batch sizing to avoid OOM, and caching so the CPU data path doesn't become what you're accidentally measuring. Documented speedups up to 325x CPU-to-GPU. The more useful finding was negative: that headline number only held under specific conditions, and realistic full-dataset workloads landed nearer 6-10x. I also caught a bug in my own memory tracking where peak values were cumulative rather than per-model.

entries.title: Medical image classification ensemble
entries.text: A multi-modal skin lesion classifier combining dermoscopic images with patient metadata. Half the job was data engineering: 134,685 raw images across nine ISIC collections, about 50% duplicates from collections repackaging each other, deduplicated down to 39,231 clean images, with splits grouped by lesion ID rather than image to prevent leakage. I trained three diverse backbones with PyTorch DDP and mixed precision, then stacked them with a logistic-regression meta-learner. The ensemble hit 84.04% accuracy, beating the best single model at 82.69% and a fine-tuned 400M-parameter medical foundation model at 81.23%, while training 4.5x faster.

entries.title: RAG and vector database backend
entries.text: I built an end-to-end RAG backend: document ingestion, embedding, vector indexing and low-latency semantic search, offline-first with locally cached models. The parts that took thought: a parser layer across PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV and Markdown where tables convert to markdown format because embedding models handle those far better than raw CSV; token-aware chunking using each model's own tokenizer rather than a fixed character count; and automatic query and passage prefix handling, since some models expect asymmetric prefixes and quietly underperform without them. Benchmarked five embedding models — the best scored 0.93 similarity on technical documents against 0.67 for the weakest.

entries.title: OWASP vulnerability detection engine
entries.text: Built during my internship: a static analysis plus LLM engine for OWASP vulnerability detection — SQL injection, RCE, XSS and related classes. Static checks run first, then flagged code goes to a language model for semantic understanding, with intent-aware parsing so it can distinguish genuinely dangerous constructs from ones that merely pattern-match, plus handling for obfuscated input. Output is human-readable explanations rather than rule IDs. What I took from it: static analysers are precise but literal, LLMs are contextual but unreliable, and the interesting engineering is the handoff between them.

entries.title: Microservices, gateway and access control
entries.text: I architected Dockerized microservices with FastAPI and role-based access control, designed for independent scaling with consistent error handling. The request path runs through a layered pipeline: middleware validates shape, content type and payload size before anything reaches business logic; session auth attaches user context; then hierarchical access enrichment resolves organisation, project and resource permissions with early exits so requests that don't need a database lookup don't pay for one. Every request carries an ID propagated through all logs, so a production issue can be traced end to end.

entries.title: Node-based workflow platform
entries.text: The platform lets users compose AI workflows as graphs of nodes — a visual editor backed by Python functions, each node a pure function with explicit validated inputs and outputs. I built domain workflows across several verticals, then led the migration from bespoke single-purpose nodes to a reusable generic system where workflows are rebuilt from configurable retrieval and LLM nodes. That cut new workflow development time by about half while making the platform accessible to non-developers. I also wrote the internal node specification so the next person doesn't reverse-engineer conventions from existing code.

entries.title: Multimodal model integration on GPUs
entries.text: A good chunk of my recent work: getting vision-language, speech recognition, text-to-speech and image-to-video models running and served on server GPUs, each exposed as a workflow node so users can chain them. Recent examples include an image-to-video pipeline working end to end, audio-driven lip-sync for talking avatars, and a conversational avatar flow where speech is transcribed, translated, re-synthesised and spoken back by a prepared avatar. This is where GPU work gets concrete — VRAM budgeting, quantisation choices, and chasing down why a model that should be fast isn't.

entries.title: Python Developer Intern (Jan – Jun 2026)
entries.text: My six-month internship, which converted to full-time. Four main things: the static analysis plus LLM engine for OWASP vulnerability detection, the end-to-end RAG backend, production workflows across multiple domains with documentation, and Dockerized microservices with role-based access control. It overlapped with my final MCA semester and placement coordinator duties, which made for a dense six months. What made it work was a small startup giving me production ownership early — the code went live, which is the fastest way to learn what matters.

entries.title: What the job taught me beyond code
entries.text: Writing for an audience — internal specs someone else has to act on, which is different from writing for yourself. Async communication: remote work means most collaboration happens in writing, so I've learned to anticipate the questions rather than require a follow-up. Reading a codebase before touching it, which the security audit forced on me. And the harder one: shipping something imperfect because users are waiting, which is a real adjustment coming from personal projects with no deadline.
